questions.prompt: Convert **/26** to a dotted-decimal subnet mask.
How many **usable host addresses** does a **/27** subnet have?
Write the CIDR prefix (e.g. `/24`) for the mask **255.255.248.0**.
questions.explain:
248 in the THIRD octet = `11111000` = 5 ones → 8+8+5 = **/21**.

Trick: 256−248 = 8 → block size 8 in the third octet.

questions.prompt: How many **/24** networks fit inside one **/20**?
questions.explain: 2^(24−20) = 2⁴ = **16**. Each extra prefix bit doubles the count of smaller networks.

questions.prompt: For **192.168.1.77/26**, what is the **network address**? (dotted decimal)
questions.explain:
Last octet 77 = **01**001101. /26 ⇒ 2 network bits in the last octet, 6 host bits.
Network = host bits→0: **01**000000 = 64 → **192.168.1.64**.
Block-size shortcut: 256−192=64 → blocks at 0, 64, 128, 192; 77 falls in the 64-block.

questions.prompt: Same subnet (**192.168.1.77/26**) — what is the **broadcast address**?

questions.source: Drill P4 — mask boundary inside 3rd octet
questions.prompt: For **172.16.45.200/21**, what is the **network address**? ⚠️ The /21 boundary is inside the THIRD octet.
questions.explain:
/21 ⇒ third octet has 5 network bits. 45 = **00101**101.
Network third octet: **00101**000 = 40 → **172.16.40.0/21** (mask 255.255.248.0).
Broadcast: 172.16.47.255; usable 172.16.40.1 – 172.16.47.254 (2046 hosts).
Block size in 3rd octet: 256−248 = 8 → blocks 40, 48… and 45 sits in the 40-block.

questions.prompt: You are given **192.168.1.4/30**. Which statement labels the four addresses of this subnet correctly?
questions.explain:
/30 ⇒ block size 4; the block containing .4 starts AT 4:
- **192.168.1.4 — network address**
- **.5, .6 — usable hosts**
- **.7 — broadcast**

*Exam tip: a /30 is the standard router-to-router link: exactly 2 usable.*

questions.prompt: A technician configures a PC as **10.130.73.95/27**. Why is this configuration **invalid**?
options: .95 is the broadcast address of subnet 10.130.73.64/27 — host bits all 1, never assignable
.95 is the network address of the subnet
/27 is not a legal prefix for a Class A address
questions.explain:
Last octet 95 = **010**11111; /27 ⇒ 3 network bits in last octet.
Network = **010**00000 = 64 → 10.130.73.64; Broadcast = **010**11111 = **95**.
**.95 IS the broadcast address** — it can never be assigned to a device. (Twin trap: .64 = network address, also unassignable.)

questions.prompt: **192.168.4.0/24** is divided into **4 equal subnets**. What is the **first usable address of Subnet 1** (the second subnet)?
**172.16.14.0/24** divided into **8 equal subnets**. Give the **subnet mask** (dotted decimal) of the new subnets.
questions.explain:
8 subnets ⇒ borrow 3 bits ⇒ **/27** = **255.255.255.224**, block size 32.
Subnet 2 starts at 2×32 = 64: network 172.16.14.64, broadcast .95, **usable .65 – .94**.

questions.prompt: **200.23.0.0/20** must be divided into **5** subnets (round up to a power of 2). After subnetting, how many **usable hosts per subnet**?
questions.explain:
Need 5 ⇒ round to 2³ = 8 subnets ⇒ borrow 3 bits ⇒ **/23** (mask 255.255.254.0).
Host bits = 32−23 = 9 ⇒ 2⁹ − 2 = **510 hosts**.
Subnets step by 2 in the 3rd octet: 200.23.0.0/23, 200.23.2.0/23 … 200.23.14.0/23 (3 spare for the future).

questions.prompt: For the address **168.23.20.35/23**, calculate its **network address**.
questions.explain:
/23 leaves the LAST bit of the 3rd octet as a host bit. 20 = 0001010**0** — 20 is even, so AND with 254 keeps it 20.
**Network = 168.23.20.0/23** (range 168.23.20.0 – 168.23.21.255).
If the 3rd octet were ODD (e.g. 21), it would round DOWN to the even number (20).

questions.prompt: VLSM design from **192.168.10.0/24**, largest-first: HR needs **50** hosts. Which subnet does HR get?
questions.explain:
50 + 2 ≤ 64 = 2⁶ ⇒ 6 host bits ⇒ **/26** (62 usable) — /27 gives only 30 (too small), /25 wastes 76.
Largest-first allocation:

| Dept | Subnet | First–Last usable |
|---|---|---|
| HR (50) | **192.168.10.0/26** | .1 – .62 |
| IT (30) | 192.168.10.64/27 | .65 – .94 |
| Sales (20) | 192.168.10.96/27 | .97 – .126 |
| Mgmt (10) | 192.168.10.128/28 | .129 – .142 |

*Trap check: IT needs 30 and /27 gives exactly 30 usable — legal. If they asked for 31, jump to /26.*

questions.prompt: An organization needs **2000 host addresses**. Which **prefix length** must its ISP allocate? (answer like `/xx`)
questions.explain:
2000 + 2 ≤ 2¹¹ = 2048 ⇒ **11 host bits** ⇒ prefix **32 − 11 = /21**.
E.g. 163.44.224.0/21 → 2046 usable: 163.44.224.1 – 163.44.231.254.
Classful would force a **Class B** (65,534 hosts) — wasting >63,000 addresses. CIDR fixes exactly this.

questions.source: Drill P14 — 2017/18 final, 10 marks (longest prefix match)
questions.explain:
The destination matches link 2's 21-bit prefix AND link 1's 24-bit prefix → **longest prefix wins → Link 1**.

*Method sentence to write in the exam: "the entry with the longest address prefix that matches the destination address is selected."*

questions.prompt: Router R: if0 → 192.168.4.0/26, if1 → 192.168.4.64/26, if2 → default (ISP). Destination **192.168.4.130** goes out of which interface?
options: if2 — no specific entry matches; falls to the default route
if1 — it is in the .64 subnet
if0 — it is in the .0 subnet
questions.explain:
192.168.4.130 lies in .128–.191 — that subnet (.128/26) is **NOT configured** on R; only .0/26 and .64/26 exist. No specific match → **if2 (default 0.0.0.0/0)**.

*This is the classic trap: don't invent a third LAN subnet that isn't in the table.*

questions.prompt: Host **192.168.4.10:4502** connects to web server **93.184.216.34:80** through NAT (WAN addr **203.0.113.5**, assigned external port **6001**). What is the (src, dst) of the datagram **after** outgoing translation?
